story:
Amelia took her rabbit, Pip, to the library in a box. Pip only ate cake. His teeth were getting very long. "I need a book," Amelia told her mother.

The library had big shelves. Amelia found a rabbit book. She opened it the wrong way, at the last page. The pictures were upside down. Her mother laughed. "Turn it around. Start at the front."

Amelia turned the book. She pointed at the marks on the page. "What are these?" "Those are words," her mother said. "They tell you things."

Amelia looked at the words. She looked at the picture. It showed a rabbit chewing grass and leaves. Pip peeked out of the box and sniffed the picture. Then he chewed the corner of the page. Crunch, crunch.

Amelia found a leaf outside. Pip chewed it all up. "More!" he seemed to say. His teeth looked a tiny bit shorter.

The librarian waved goodbye. "Come back soon," she said. Amelia waved back. "Books tell rabbit things!"

Scarlett woke up from her nap and rubbed her eyes. She felt tired still, so she sat on her bed. Then she heard a funny sound. Grrrumble. It came from her own tummy. She put her hands on it. Grrrumble again.

"Mommy, my tummy is talking!" she called. Mommy came and held her hand. "Let's go to the kitchen," Mommy said. Scarlett stayed close to Mommy in the hall. In the kitchen, Scarlett saw the big pot on the stove. She knew it was hot, so she did not touch it. She touched the cold milk cup instead. "Cold," she said. Mommy gave her a bowl of rice. Scarlett ate it all up, slowly, bite by bite.

Then her tummy was quiet. Scarlett rolled up her sleeve and looked at her tummy. "It growled because it was empty," she said. Mommy smiled. "Now it is full." Scarlett patted her tummy gently. "All done, little tummy," she whispered. "Time to roll out the play dough." She climbed down from her chair and ran to get it.

Aubrey sat at the dinner table. There was soup in her bowl. But Aubrey had a problem. The soup was too hot. "I can't eat it," she said. She was lucky, because Daddy had an idea. "Bang the drum," he said. He tapped the little drum on the table. Boom, boom, boom. Aubrey put her hand on the drum. She felt it shake. "The drum is shaking!" she said. She put her hand on her ear. Her ear was shaking too, a tiny bit. Aubrey tapped the drum. Boom. Her ear shook again. She stopped tapping. Her ear was still. "When the drum shakes, my ear shakes!" she said. Daddy smiled. "The wiggles pass through the air," he said. "Then your ear shakes. That is how you hear."

Aubrey looked at her soup. She saw the steam rise up. She smelled it with her nose. Yum, it smelled like carrots. Then she touched the bowl. It was warm now, not hot. She counted on her fingers, "One, two, three." The soup was ready. She took a little taste with her tongue. "Warm and good!" she said. Aubrey ate her soup, one spoon at a time. Then she tapped the drum one more time. Boom. "I hear it," said Aubrey. "My ear is shaking again."

Livia went to the art gallery with Papa. She saw a big red painting. "Red," she said. Then a big yellow one. "Yellow!" Then a blue one. "Blue!" She wanted to paint too. Papa found a table with red and yellow paint. There was a noisy kitchen next to it. A baker said, "Come and see my bread." The dough was in a big bowl. Livia watched. The dough grew and grew, like a balloon. Livia thought it was alive. She chased a little bubble up the side of the bowl. "Look, Papa! Bubbles!" The baker said the yeast, a tiny living thing, ate sugar in the dough and made the bubbles. Livia touched the dough. It felt soft, not yucky at all. Then she mixed red and yellow paint. It turned orange, just like the bread! "The bubbles make it big," said Livia. The baker smiled and gave her a warm slice to eat.

Thomas ran to the bathroom. He wanted to wash his cookie hands. Mama came with him.

Thomas touched the faucet. It was rough and old. "Careful," said Mama. "The red side is hot."

Thomas turned the blue side. Cold water ran out. He rubbed his hands. They got clean.

Then the water got warm. Thomas felt hot. Water ran down his face. "I am all wet, Mama!" he said.

"That is sweat," said Mama. "Your skin has tiny holes. They let out sweat. As it dries, it cools you down."

Thomas felt his arm. The sweat was drying. His arm felt cool.

"The water made me hot," said Thomas. "The sweat made me cool!"

Mama smiled. "Good thinking. Now do not touch the red side. And do not forget your towel."

Thomas took the soft towel. He patted his arms. Cool and dry. "All done, Mama!"

Then they went back for one more cookie.

Nora wanted to wear her coat all by herself. She put one arm in. Then the other arm. The zipper was hard. "I can do it," she said. She pushed the little pull. One tooth, two teeth, three teeth. Then it stuck. Papa knelt down. He held the bottom for her. Nora pushed again. One tooth, two teeth, three teeth, four. Zip! The coat was closed.

Before they went out, Nora washed her hands. A bit of tissue fell in the toilet. She pushed the handle. The water made a loud rush. It went from the tank into the bowl. The rushing water pulled the tissue down the pipe. "It went down," said Nora. "The water pulled it."

Then they ran outside. "Let's pretend we are sheep," said Nora. "Baa, baa, baa!" Papa laughed. They hopped over the grass together.

Miles went to the library with his dad. They came on the bus. Miles held his heavy bag of books. He wanted to draw on the library tablet. He did not know how to turn it on. Miss Amy, the kind librarian, showed him the little button. Miles pressed it. The screen lit up. He tapped the drawing app and made a red cat.

Then Miles walked past the little fridge by the juice cups. He put his hand on the back of it. "It feels warm," he said. "Is the fridge broken?" He asked Miss Amy. She smiled and shook her head. Miles felt the front. It was cold. He felt the back again. It was warm. He thought and thought. "Warm goes out the back," he said. "Cold stays inside. That is why the juice is cold." He tapped his head. "The fridge pushes the warm out!" Then it was time to go. Miles hung his coat on his hook. He pressed the button and the tablet went dark. "Bye bye, tablet," he said. He waved at Miss Amy. "I can do it all by myself next time."

Cooper made a picture for Grandma. It had a big red sun. He wanted to mail it all by himself.

Daddy helped him fold the paper. Cooper put it in an envelope. He licked the sticker and pressed it shut. Then they walked down the wet street to the big blue mailbox. Cooper slipped the letter into the slot. It fell down inside with a soft sound.

The next day, the mail carrier came to their house. She gave the letter back. "There is no address on it," she said. "I take letters to a big building. Then they go to the address written on them. This one has no address, so it came back here."

Cooper looked at the envelope. It was empty of words. Just his picture inside. "It needs Grandma's street," he said. Daddy nodded. They sat at the table. Daddy wrote Grandma's address, and Cooper drew a little stamp in the corner. His sister Lily wanted to hold the envelope. "You hold it first," Cooper said. "Then me." Lily held it. Then Cooper held it. Then Cooper held it again. "My turn," said Lily. Cooper gave it back. "Okay. Your turn," he said.

They walked to the mailbox together. Cooper slipped the letter in. The mail carrier came the next day. She took the big bag of letters away. In three days, the phone rang. It was Grandma. "My sun picture came!" she said. Cooper smiled big.

Sara went to the library with Dad. Story time was about wild animals, and Sara felt excited. She sat on a small red mat.

A boy named Ben sat next to her. Ben had a scab on his knee. He picked at it. Then the scab came off. The cut opened again. A little dot of blood came out. Ben looked sad and scared. He wanted to cry.

Sara looked at the scab in his hand. "Put it back," she said. "The scab is a lid. New skin grows under it."

Ben put a tissue on his knee. The librarian came to help. She gave Ben a bandage.

"I will tell Dad," said Ben. "The library has a store of bandages!"

"Good," said Sara. Then story time began. A lion roared on the page. Sara clapped her hands.

Declan got to daycare, but the yard looked different. It was all white and soft. "Where did the sky go?" he asked. Miss Jo smiled. "It is fog," she said. "It came down low." Declan wanted to touch a cloud. Clouds were way up high. That was his problem. But the fog was right here. He put out his hand. His fingers went into the white. It felt cool and damp. He walked in it. He was walking in a cloud! "My socks are wet," he said. The wet would stick to his shoes too. "Yesterday the sun was out," said Miss Jo. "Today we have fog. Tomorrow the sun may come back." Declan nodded. "Now I touch a cloud. Later I will tell Mom." He held his hand up high, all the way home.

Charlie stood on her little stool in the kitchen. She wanted to make breakfast all by herself. "Can I do the toast today?" she asked. Mom smiled and said, "Yes, let us try."

The butter was cold and hard. Charlie tried to spread it. The butter made a hole in the soft bread. "Hmm," said Charlie. "The butter is too hard. What will help?" Mom set the toast near the warm stove. Soon the butter went soft. Charlie spread it in thin, smooth lines. "Look!" she said. "Soft butter spreads easy."

Next came the milk. Charlie poured slowly, slowly. One drop ran down the side of the cup. She wiped it with a cloth. Then she poured again. This time not one drop spilled. "I did it," she said.

Then Ben came in. He saw six cookies on the plate. "I want more than you," said Ben. "No, me!" said Charlie. They both reached. Mom said, "Count them out." They took turns. One for Ben, one for Charlie. Two for Ben, two for Charlie. Three for Ben, three for Charlie. The plate was empty. Charlie held up her cookies. "Same same!" she said. "Three and three. Now let us eat."

Madeline turned three today. Grandma's house smelled like cake. Everyone sat at the big table.

Grandpa said, "We need more balloons. Let's go to the store." Madeline put on her cool new shoes. They were blue with stars.

At the store, Madeline saw the balloons. She grabbed them. "Free!" she said.

Grandpa shook his head. He put coins in the shop lady's hand. The lady smiled and gave him the balloons.

"You give money, you get things," Madeline said.

"Yes," said Grandpa. "The lady keeps the money. She buys more things to sell. And she pays the people who help her."

Madeline held the coins from her birthday card. She picked out one pink balloon. She gave her coins to the lady.

"Here you go," said the lady.

Back home, Madeline sat in Grandma's soft chair. The balloon bobbed by her head. It went squeak on her nose.

"Balloons because I paid!" said Madeline.

Maria ran to the backyard in her new hat. The sun was hot. She played by the flowers. Then she felt water on her nose. She wiped it with her hand.

"Oh no," said Maria. "Is something wrong with me?"

Mama sat on the step. "Come sit with me," she said. Maria sat close to Mama. They waited in the shade. Maria felt the water dry on her arms. Slowly, slowly, she felt cooler.

"Sweat dries and cools me down," said Maria. "That is what it does."

Then Maria saw the red grill in the corner. "Is it hot?" she asked. "Yes, it is hot," said Mama. "We do not touch it." Maria kept her hands away. She sat and waited some more.

The sweat dried. Maria felt cool. "Mama, sweat dries and cools me down," she said again. Mama smiled. Maria held her hat and ran one more lap, close to Mama, cool as can be.

Alice went to the store with her brother Sam. They saw apples in a big row. "One, two, three, four, five," said Alice. She liked saying the numbers. Then she saw cookies in a jar. Ten cookies sat in a little bag. "Can we get them?" she asked. Mama said yes.

Alice and Sam got hungry on the walk home. They sat on a bench. Alice held the bag. Sam grabbed it too. "I want more!" said Sam. "No, me!" said Alice. Then Alice had an idea. "Let's try counting them out," she said. She put one cookie on her knee. Then one on Sam's knee. She kept going, one and one, all the way to six.

The bag was empty of cookies now. Alice looked at her pile. "One, two, three," she said. Sam counted his too. "One, two, three!" He smiled. Alice laughed. "Six cookies, and we both got three!" They ate their cookies in the sun. "That's why counting helped," said Alice. Sam licked his crumbs and nodded.

Lydia skipped to the big stadium with Dad. They came to watch the last game of the year. "One, two, three, four seats," said Lydia. Dad, Grandma, Milo, and Lydia. All four sat down. Lydia's tummy was happy. She had a snack.

On Lydia's knee was a little scab. It was from a fall. She wanted to pick it off. "I want to see under it," she said. She picked at one edge. Grandma held her hand. "Leave the lid on," said Grandma. Lydia sat on her hands. She clapped for the players. She jumped up. She sat down.

The game ended. The crowd cheered loud. "We won! We won!" said Milo. Lydia looked at her knee. The scab was gone now. It had fallen off by itself. Under it was new pink skin. "Look, Grandma! The lid came off. New skin!" Grandma smiled. Lydia patted her soft knee and waved at the field.

Emilia went to the store with Dad. She wanted to send Grandma a picture. It was a present for Grandma's birthday. Emilia drew a big red heart, deep red like a strawberry.

They stood in line at the mail counter. A man was first. Then a lady. Then it was Emilia's turn. "My turn now," she said. Dad helped her drop the letter in the mail slot.

Then Emilia looked at her letter. It had no name on it. No house on it. Dad said, "The mail carrier takes the letter to a big building. Then it goes to the address on it." Emilia's eyes got big. Her letter had no address!

Dad asked the lady at the counter for help. The lady smiled and got the letter back. Emilia wrote her name. Dad wrote Grandma's house. The letter went in again. "Bye, letter," said Emilia. "Go to Grandma!"

Chloe wanted to give her rabbit, Bib, a bite of cake. "No cake for Bib," said Grandma. "Rabbits eat grass and leaves and plants." Chloe pouted. "Cake is yummy," said Chloe. Bib sniffed the cake with his little nose. "That is his nose," said Chloe. "He smells the cake!" Bib did not eat the cake. He nibbled a crunchy carrot instead. "Listen," said Chloe. "I hear him crunch with his ears." Then she looked at Bib's teeth. "Grandma! His teeth are so long!" "They never stop growing," said Grandma. "So Bib chews tough plants to wear them down." Chloe picked a big leaf. Bib chewed and chewed. "His teeth need the leaf," said Chloe. She touched his soft fur. "I feel his fuzzy back!" Bib twitched his nose at her. "I smell cake," said Chloe. She took a big bite.

Andrew was at the lake pool. He was shy about the water. "I want to swim like Dad," he said. Dad held his hands. "Let's try a little kick," said Dad. Andrew kicked. Splash! He tried again. Splash, splash!

A drum sat by the pool. A boy hit it. Boom! Andrew put his hand on the drum. The drum was shaking! Then he heard the boom in his ear. He put his hand on his ear. His ear was shaking too, a tiny bit. "My ear is like the drum," said Andrew. "The sound makes it shake!" Dad smiled. "Yes, the wiggles of sound make it shake."

Andrew kicked some more. He waited, then kicked again. Pop! A bubble came up by his toes. "I made a bubble!" After his swim, Andrew took a nap under a big tree. He dreamed of drums, ears, and splashing.

Chloe wanted toast and milk all by herself. "I can do it," she said. She took the butter knife. The butter was cold and hard. She pushed it on the toast. The toast tried to slip off the plate. Chloe held it with one finger. "Stay there, toast," she said. The butter went on, bit by bit.

Then she poured the milk. She poured too fast at first. A little milk ran over. "Oops," said Daddy with a smile. Chloe poured slowly next time. Not one drop ran over. The cup was full.

Daddy put crackers on her plate. Chloe looked at them. "This one has three corners," she said. "It's a triangle." She held up another. "This one has four corners. It's a square." She spread butter on the square cracker. She bit it. "The square tastes like toast too," she said. Outside the window the sky looked stormy and gray. Chloe sipped her milk and watched the rain run down the wall of the house. "Good job, Chloe," said Daddy. Chloe held up her cup. "More milk, please!"

Emilia went to the clinic with Dad. She stood in a long line. She counted the people. "One, two, three, four!" she said. "I am number five!"

A nurse came out with a big pot of soup. She had cut an onion for it in the back room. Dad's eyes got wet. Tears ran down his face.

Emilia felt worried. "Are you sad because I get a shot?" she asked. "No," said Dad. He held the onion peel up to his nose. More tears came. Then he put it far away and wiped his eyes. The tears stopped!

"The onion makes tears come," Emilia said. "Even when you are not sad!"

Then it was her turn. Emilia looked away and counted to three. The nurse said, "All done!"

Emilia jumped up. "That shot made my arm just a little weak!" she said. "Ice cream will fix it!" Dad laughed. They ran out to the car.
